en.intro: The worm-eating warbler (Helmitheros vermivorum) is a small New World warbler that breeds in the Eastern United States and migrates to southern Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America for the winter. It is the only species in the genus Helmitheros.

sections.Description: The worm-eating warbler is a small New World warbler. It is around 13 cm (5.1 in) in length and weighs 11.8–17.4 g (0.42–0.61 oz). It is relatively plain with olive-brown upperparts and light-coloured underparts, but has black and light brown stripes on its head. It has a slim pointed bill and pink legs. In immature birds, the head stripes are brownish. The male's song is a short high-pitched trill. This bird's call is a chip or tseet. Worm-eating warblers are sexually monomorphic. Males and females can only reliably be sexed during the breeding season by the presence of a brood patch in females or a cloacal protuberance in males. These birds are also difficult to age. Hatch year/second year birds have rusty tips on tertials that wear off by March of the following year. Juveniles can be distinguished by duskier head markings, and cinnamon wingbars.
sections.Distribution and habitat:
These birds breed in the Eastern United States. Their selected habitats vary significantly between populations. In much of their range, worm-eating warblers are associated with mature hardwood forests on steep slopes. However, recent attention has been focused on coastal breeding populations, as little is known about their ecology or status. Historically, coastal populations would select for pocosin ecosystems. More recently, however, these populations have shifted to frequent use of pine plantations. Current use of pine plantations has resulted in densities higher than in areas previously thought to be their natural habitat. This shift in habitat selection likely demonstrates that worm-eating warblers are more closely associated with shrub structure than stand age or size. If this is the case, the landscape changes that occurred on the Atlantic coastal plain may have had less of an impact on these birds than previously described. Maintaining this species habitat may require managing for dense shrubby midstory and understory. Due to their reliance on shrub structure for foraging, and ground nesting behavior, frequent fires have a negative impact on this species. Other management strategies that reduce the shrub mid-story, increase herbaceous growth, and decrease canopy cover are likely to have a similar effect. More information is needed about their breeding habits in coastal regions as these forests are likely to represent different conditions from their inland counterparts. Fat deposits play a key role in allowing for long-distance migration in most passerines. Stopover habitat, or areas that allow birds to replenish their fat stores, are also critical.
In winter, these birds migrate to southern Mexico, the Greater Antilles, and Central America particularly along the Caribbean Slope where they occupy both scrub and moist forests. Worm-eating warblers have disappeared from some parts of their range due to habitat loss but their ability to use both scrub and moist forest ecosystems may be beneficial to the long term conservation of this species.

Breeding
This bird breeds in dense deciduous forests in the eastern United States, usually on wooded slopes. The nest is an open cup placed on the ground, hidden among dead leaves. It is one of several species of new-world warblers that nests on the ground including the black-and-white warbler (Mniotilta varia), the ovenbird (Seiurus aurocapilla), the northern waterthrush (Parkesia noveboracensis), Louisiana waterthrush (Parkesia motacilla), palm warbler (Setophaga palmarum), and the Kentucky warbler (Geothlypis formosa). The female lays four or five eggs. Both parents feed the young; they may try to distract predators near the nest by pretending to be injured. Worm-eating warblers are often parasitized by brown-headed cowbirds (Molothrus ater) where forest fragmentation occurs. Reducing forest fragmentation may prove vital if populations of worm-eating warblers suffer large declines.

Food and feeding
The diet of worm-eating warblers varies across habitat types. This variation can be attributed to different predator avoidance strategies employed by common prey items. On their breeding grounds, worm-eating warblers glean mostly from live foliage, searching for arthropods. On the wintering grounds, this species gleans insects almost exclusively from dead plant material. The name "worm-eating" refers to the numerous Lepidopteran larvae that this species consumes; they rarely if ever eat earthworms.
Use of pesticides, especially those broadcast over a wide area, is likely to have an effect on most insectivorous songbird species, including the worm-eating warbler. These pesticides decrease the species' primary food source and could result in long-term toxicity.
sections.Taxonomy: The worm-eating warbler was formally described in 1789 by the German naturalist Johann Friedrich Gmelin in his revised and expanded edition of Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae. He placed it with the wagtails in the genus Motacilla and coined the binomial name Motacilla vermivora. Gmelin based his account on the "worm-eater" that had been described and illustrated in 1760 by the English naturalist George Edwards in his Gleanings of Natural History. Edwards had received a specimen from the American naturalist William Bartram that had been collected in Pennsylvania. The worm-eating warbler is now placed in the genus Helmitheros that was introduced in 1819 by the French polymath Constantine Samuel Rafinesque. The genus name combines the Ancient Greek helmins meaning "worm", and -thēras meaning "hunter". The specific epithet vermivorum is from Latin vermis meaning "worm" and -vorus meaning "-eating". The species is monotypic: no subspecies are recognised.

es.intro: La reinita gusanera​ (Helmitheros vermivorum) es una especie de ave paseriforme de la familia Parulidae, la única perteneciente al género monotípico Helmitheros. Es un ave migratoria que anida en el este de América del Norte y que inverna en México, América Central e islas del Caribe.

sections.Distribución y hábitat:
cría en la mayor parte de la región de los Apalaches, ausente en el valle del río Misisipi, pero vuelve a aparecer al oeste del río en el norte de Luisiana, Arkansas, sur y centro de Misisipi, sureste de Oklahoma, extremo este de Texas. Al este del valle del río Misisipi, se reproduce localmente en el norte y centro de Misisipi,norte y suroeste de Alabama, norte de Georgia y montañas del oeste de Carolina del Sur, oeste de Carolina del Norte y oeste de Virginia; su principal área de reproducción se extiende hacia el norte por el centro y el este de Tennessee y por Kentucky, Virginia Occidental y Maryland hasta el extremo sur de Indiana, sureste de Ohio, Pensilvania, noroeste de Nueva Jersey, sureste de Nueva York, Connecticut, oeste y norte de Rhode Island  y suroeste y sureste de Massachusetts.​
En los inviernos boreales migra hacia el sur ocupando desde el este y oeste de México hacia el sur por Belice, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica hasta Panamá; en el Caribe en Bahamas, islas Caimán, Cuba,  República Dominicana, Haití, Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Islas Turcas y Caicos e Islas Vírgenes; se registra su presencia como vagante invernal en Antigua y Barbuda, Anguila, Guadalupe y Martinica, y muy raramente en el norte de América del Sur en Colombia y Venezuela; y como vagante estival en Canadá y San Pedro y Miquelón.​
Esta especie aparece regularmente en sus hábitats preferenciales: las grandes extensiones de bosque maduro caducifolio o mixto caducifolio-conífero se solapan con laderas y pequeños parches de arbustos como el laurel de montaña (Kalmia latifolia) y el rododendro (Rhododendron maximum). Considerada una especie de interior de bosque, poco común en pequeños parches de bosque dentro de paisajes forestales fragmentados.​ Durante la invernada es reportado en una gran variedad de ambientes boscosos.​

Descripción original
La especie H. vermivorum fue descrita por primera vez por el naturalista alemán Gmelin en 1789 bajo el nombre científico Motacilla vermivora; su localidad tipo es: «Pensilvania», restringido posteriormente para «Filadelfia, Pensilvania».​ 
El género Helmitheros fue propuesto por el naturalista francés Constantine Samuel Rafinesque en 1819, que en la misma publicación describió a la especie tipo Helmitheros migratorius, en realidad un sinónimo posterior de Motacilla vermivora, actualmente Helmitheros vermivorum.​

Etimología
El nombre genérico neutro «Helmitheros» se compone de la palabras del griego «helmins» que significa ‘gusano’, y «thēras» que significa ‘cazador’; y el nombre de la especie «vermivorum» se compone de las palabras del latín «vermis» que significa ‘gusano’ y «vorus» que significa ‘comer’.​

Taxonomía
Es monotípica.​

Bibliografía
Peterson, R.T. & Chalif, E.L. (2008) Aves de México. Guía de campo. Editorial Diana, México. ISBN 9789681332075
sections.Nombres comunes: Aparte de reinita gusanera (en Costa Rica, Panamá, Puerto Rico, Venezuela y Colombia), se le denomina también bijirita gusanera (en Cuba), chipe gusanero o chipe vermívoro​ (en México), cigüita cabeza rayada (en la República Dominicana), chipe comegusanos (en Honduras) o reinita anteada (en Nicaragua).​
